Custom Millwork

The handcrafted details that turn a house into something people remember.

What This Is

Millwork Is the Art of Finishing a Room Right.

Millwork is everything made from wood that defines the architectural detail of a room — crown molding, baseboards, chair rails, wainscoting, coffered ceilings, built-in columns, door casings, and decorative trim. It's what separates a house that feels complete from one that feels unfinished.

North Star custom-fabricates millwork to match your home's existing architecture or to establish a new character entirely. Everything we make is built by hand to fit your exact space — no off-the-shelf profiles, no filler pieces, no visible gaps.

What's Included

Everything That Belongs on the Wall, Ceiling, or Floor Edge.

  • Crown molding & cornice work
  • Wainscoting & paneling
  • Coffered & tray ceilings
  • Chair rails & picture rails
  • Door & window casings
  • Baseboards & shoe molding
  • Decorative columns & pilasters
  • Built-in niches & display frames
Why It Matters

You'll Pass This On to Your Kids.

Custom millwork isn't a trend. It's an investment in the permanent character of your home. When it's done right — and we mean every miter tight, every profile consistent, every finish smooth — it's the kind of detail that a future buyer notices immediately and a future appraiser adds to the value column without hesitation.

Our Process
1

Measure & Match

We measure every wall, corner, and run — then match or create the molding profile that fits your home.

2

Custom Fabrication

We fabricate the millwork pieces to spec — no standard profiles that almost fit.

3

Installation

We install clean, tight, and level — every joint mitered, every nail set and filled.

4

Prime & Paint-Ready

We leave everything primed and ready for your painter — or we can handle that too.

A full kitchen remodel means we start fresh. We strip it down, rethink the layout if needed, and rebuild everything — from the cabinets to the countertops to the backsplash to the floor. Nothing gets left the way it was unless you want it that way.

Wood Floors

Real hardwood floors outlast trends, furniture, and bad decisions.

What This Is

The Single Best Investment You Can Make in Your Home's Floors.

Hardwood floors don't go out of style. They don't get dated the way tile patterns do. They get sanded, restained, and refinished — and they look new again. That's why appraisers add them to value columns and buyers add them to search filters. A well-installed hardwood floor is a 50-year decision.

North Star installs solid hardwood, engineered hardwood, and handles refinishing of existing wood floors. We help you choose the right species, width, and finish — and we sand, stain, and coat it to the level it deserves.

What's Included
  • Solid hardwood installation
  • Engineered hardwood installation
  • Floor sanding & refinishing
  • Stain application (custom colors)
  • Poly & oil finish coatings

Advice

5 Questions to Ask Before Hiring a Renovation Contractor

Most homeowners hire the wrong contractor not because they didn't look hard enough — but because they asked the wrong questions. Here's what to ask, and more importantly, what the answers tell you.

1. Are you licensed and insured in New York and Connecticut?

This is the non-negotiable. If a contractor can't show you a license number, a certificate of insurance, and proof that their workers are covered — stop the conversation there. In New York, you can verify a contractor's license through the state licensing board. A licensed contractor isn't just legal. They're accountable.

Red flag: "We're working on getting the license" or "Insurance costs too much." Walk away.

2. Who is on site every day?

Some contractors sell you on themselves — then send a crew of people you've never met. Ask point-blank: "Who physically shows up at my home, and will I be able to reach them?" A good contractor has a real answer. At North Star, Raymundo is on every project. You have his cell number. That's the deal.

Red flag: "I have a foreman who handles the day-to-day." Ask to meet the foreman before you sign anything.

3. Do you use subcontractors? Which ones?

Subcontracting isn't automatically bad — but you deserve to know who's coming into your home. Ask which parts of the project will be subcontracted, and whether those subs are licensed and insured. An honest contractor will tell you exactly who does what.

4. What's in writing?

Everything should be. Scope of work, materials with brand/model numbers, timeline with milestones, payment schedule, and what happens if something changes mid-project. A one-page "contract" that just says "Kitchen remodel - $18,000" is not a contract. It's a setup for conflict.

5. Can I see past work — and talk to past clients?

Photos are easy to find or borrow. References are not. Any contractor who's been doing good work for years has clients who will take a five-minute phone call to tell you about it. If they can't produce three recent references in the same type of project, that's a signal.

Not sure where to start?

Call Raymundo. He'll answer your questions honestly — even if the answer is that we're not the right fit.

Kitchens

Kitchen Remodel vs. Kitchen Refresh: Which One Do You Actually Need?

Not every unhappy kitchen needs a gut renovation. But some refreshes end up costing more than a full remodel once you add up the piecemeal decisions. Here's how to tell the difference before you spend a dollar.

What a Refresh Covers

A kitchen refresh means keeping the bones — the layout, the cabinet boxes, the plumbing locations — and updating the surfaces. New cabinet fronts or paint, new hardware, new countertops, new backsplash, maybe new lighting. Done right, a refresh can transform a tired kitchen for $8,000-15,000 in Westchester.

What a Full Remodel Covers

A full remodel means opening the walls, reconfiguring the layout, replacing cabinet boxes, relocating plumbing or electrical, and essentially rebuilding the entire space. You're looking at $30,000-80,000+ depending on scope, materials, and what's behind the walls when you open them up.

The Decision Checklist

Consider a refresh if: your layout works, your cabinet boxes are solid, your plumbing and electrical are in good shape, and you're updating for aesthetics rather than function.

Consider a full remodel if: your layout doesn't work for how you cook, your cabinet boxes are failing, you want to open up the space, or you're already doing other major renovation work nearby.

Honest Westchester truth: Most kitchens built before 2000 have cabinet boxes that are tired. What looks like a refresh candidate often turns into a remodel once you start pulling things apart. Build that possibility into your budget conversation.

Not sure which your kitchen needs?

Raymundo can walk through it with you in 20 minutes and tell you what's worth keeping and what isn't.

Flooring

Why Westchester Homeowners Are Choosing Hardwood Over Tile in 2025

Tile was everywhere for a decade. Gray large-format porcelain, specifically. It's durable, it photographs well, and contractors love it because it's fast to install. But the shift is real — Westchester homeowners are choosing hardwood again, and the reasons make sense.

The Warmth Factor

Hardwood is warm. Not temperature-warm — emotionally warm. Tile, no matter how beautiful, reads as cold and institutional once you've lived with it for a few years. Wood reads as home. That difference shows up in how buyers feel when they walk through a listing.

Resale Value Is Real

Hardwood floors consistently appear in buyer search filters. "Hardwood floors" is a feature buyers seek out and pay for. In Westchester, where homes are expensive and buyers are discerning, quality hardwood is a line item that appraisers and buyers both recognize.

The Maintenance Reality Check

Tile is forgiving with water. Hardwood requires more attention in wet areas. But in living rooms, dining rooms, hallways, and bedrooms — which is most of your home — hardwood is no harder to maintain than tile and infinitely easier to repair. Scratch a tile and you're replacing tiles. Scratch hardwood and you sand and refinish.

Ready to install hardwood floors?

Exterior

What a Deck Addition Really Adds to Your Home (It's More Than You Think)

A deck isn't just somewhere to put patio furniture. It's usable square footage, it's lifestyle, and in Westchester — it's significant resale value. Here's the full picture before you decide whether to build.

ROI on Decks in Westchester

The national average ROI on a new deck is 65-75% at resale. In Westchester, where outdoor space is at a premium and buyers are accustomed to paying for quality, that number trends higher. A $20,000 deck can add $15,000-18,000 to a home's sale price in this market — which isn't pure profit, but it's far better than a renovation that adds zero.

The Lifestyle Value Is the Real Number

The ROI calculation assumes you sell immediately after building. Most people don't. They live with the deck for 5-10 years first. The lifestyle value — dinners outside, kids having somewhere to play, having a space that makes your home feel bigger — doesn't show up on a spreadsheet, but it's real.

What to Build It With

Pressure-treated wood is the budget option and works fine. Composite decking (Trex, TimberTech) costs more upfront but requires almost zero maintenance. Hardwood decking (Ipe, cedar) is beautiful and durable. We'll walk you through the tradeoffs on-site.

The Permit Process

Yes, decks require permits in Westchester and Connecticut. North Star handles the permit process on every deck project. Don't let a contractor tell you permits aren't necessary — they are, and building without them creates problems at sale time that are expensive to fix.

Carpentry

The Real Story Behind Custom Millwork — Why It's Worth Every Penny

Custom millwork looks expensive. It also lasts 50 years, adds serious resale value, and makes your home look like it was designed by someone who actually cared. Here's what goes into it — and why the price is what it is.

What Millwork Actually Is

Millwork is the term for architectural woodwork that defines a room's character — crown molding, wainscoting, coffered ceilings, chair rails, built-in columns, decorative trim. It's the detail work. The stuff that separates a room that photographs beautifully from one that looks like it was finished by the builder in a hurry.

Mass-Produced vs. Custom: What's the Difference?

The home improvement store sells trim in 8-foot sticks that you cut to fit. It works. It looks fine. Custom millwork is fabricated to your exact space — matching existing profiles, running continuously without joints, sized and scaled to your ceiling height and room proportions. You can feel the difference before you can name it.

What It Costs and Why

Custom millwork costs more than stock trim because it takes more time, more skill, and more material. A coffered ceiling in a 14x16 dining room might cost $4,000-8,000 depending on complexity. A wainscoting run through an entryway might be $1,500-3,000. These are not decorating expenses. They're permanent improvements that appraisers recognize and buyers specifically look for.

Where to Use It First

If you're adding millwork for the first time: start in the room that matters most — the foyer (first impression), the dining room (most photographed), or the living room. Crown molding throughout a home is the single most cost-effective millwork project most homeowners can do.

Want to see what it would look like in your home?

Raymundo has been building custom millwork for years. He can tell you exactly what will work in your space and what it will cost.
